The words stress, accent, prominence and pitch do not occur anywhere in the 37-page article (full-text search of the scan: 0 hits). The only prominence-adjacent remarks are vowel note 7 on p. 30, 'In prefixes, vowels are weak and indistinct.', and the word-formation section on p. 37, which calls prefixes 'reduced syllables' that 'only contain simple vowels without finals'. 4451.dq: As a general structural pattern, the reflexes of the inherited Proto Mirndi prefixes can be reconstructed as bearing primary word-level stress in Proto Yirram. ... In productive prefixation systems in Australian languages, primary stress is preferentially on the root. Consequently, in words consisting of a monosyllabic prefix + polysyllabic root, the stress is on the first syllable of the root.
4451.dloc: p. 78, §7.4, ex. (208) and the following paragraph (p. 88 of the ANU file); supporting p. 28 'The acute accent indicates primary stress' and p. 29 ex. (74)-(75); pp. 83-84 tables (214)-(216) with stress-marked Nungali subsection terms.
4451.heavy: No weight rule stated. The only weight/onset mention is the exception at p. 29: a root whose 'initial syllable... is light and its onset is an approximant' fails to attract stress.
4451.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the root; a monosyllabic prefix before a polysyllabic root (outer noun-class ti-/nya-/ni-, pronominal nga-) is unstressed, stress being 'preferentially on the root': Nung ti-y-úrla, ti-y-ámirra, nya-n-ámirra, ni-y-úya. A former prefix that has been lexicalised into the stem carries the stress as the stem-initial syllable (nya-ná-yipi, nya-ná-wurla, ni-ná-wuya, tí-y-imij, nyá-na-mij). Position is therefore set by morphological structure (prefix vs root/stem), not by a count from the word edge.

4452.prule: Stress on the penultimate syllable of the base (Grundwort), the inherited Ur-Ambon rule. In Nusalaut the accent has moved toward the word end where a further monosyllabic suffix followed the support vowel (nuwól-lo < *nuwól-o-lo) and with the verbal suffixes -e and -lo (palá-e, tomá-lo, iló-lo), i.e. onto the penult of the suffixed word; the nominal ending -lo does not move the accent (háu-lo, móti-lo, usál-ljo), but its vowel is mostly lost (lá'u-l, húwa-l, muláha-l), so the surface position is again the penult. van Hoëvell 1877: 'in den regel valt op de voorlaatste lettergreep' for the five dialects incl. Nusalaut, stressed vowel long.

4453.dq: In Tsishaath Nootka stress assignment the domain of primary stress is the first two syllables of the word (i.e., the first foot). (p. 58)
4453.dloc: p. 58, ch. 6 §6.2 'The Status of Tsishaath Nootka Stress' (opening sentence); restated p. 60 before rule (10).
4453.heavy: 'either a long vowel or a vowel-sonorant sequence consist of two moras' (p. 59): heavy = long vowel (V:) or short vowel + tautosyllabic sonorant/nasal coda; 'when there is an obstruent in the coda, there is no effect on the placement of stress' (p. 59); VʔV sequences 'behave as a single, long vowel' and may outrank heavy syllables (p. 60).
4453.dflt: first syllable ('if both syllables are light, stress the leftmost one in the first foot', p. 60; data (5) tánanak, náyaqak)
4453.prule: Primary stress is confined to the first two syllables of the word (the initial foot). Stress the leftmost heavy syllable within that window; if both are light, stress the first. So: #H́L, #H́H, #ĹL, #LH́. Heavy = long vowel, or short vowel plus a tautosyllabic sonorant (nasal) coda; obstruent codas are irrelevant; long vowels beyond the second syllable never take primary stress.
4453.srule: Secondary stresses occur beyond the initial foot; Stonham tentatively places them on alternating syllables counted from the primary stress, following the disyllabic foot structure, and says their placement 'remains to be clearly worked out'. The first vowel of a VʔV sequence attracts (primary or secondary) stress anywhere in the word.

4457.prule: No word-stress rule. Nyamwezi is a two-tone (H/L) language with high-tone shift (Schadeberg 1991; Kanijo 2019). Dahl 1904, the only source with an explicit 'accent' statement, first gives the positions of the pitch Hochton ('Die eigentlichen Töne', pp. 106-120) and then says the dynamic Haupt- and Nebenakzent 'can be found on any syllable' (ultima to 6th-last); the most frequent placement is main accent on the penult and secondary on the ultima (so the prefix takes the main accent with a monosyllabic stem), followed by six further listed combinations. No computable position is stated; the accent is not shown to be independent of tone.
4457.srule: Dahl 1904: every word with a main accent also carries one secondary accent (Nebenakzent); monosyllables carry neither. The secondary may fall on any syllable from the ultima to the fifth-from-last. Most often it is on the ultima with the main accent on the penult (disyllabic words/stems; with a monosyllabic word-final stem the prefix has the main accent and the stem the secondary). Other common combinations (p. 122, groups I-VI): main antepenult + secondary ultima; main antepenult + secondary penult; secondary antepenult + main penult; main fourth-from-last + secondary penult (full reduplications); further combinations and 5th/6th-last placements pp. 125-126. No alternating rhythm is described.

4462.dloc: §5 'Pitch-accent and Stress', p. 16 (fn. 12 on the same page); §3b 'Vowel Quantity', p. 10.
4462.prule: Weak, non-contrastive stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word, independent of pitch and blind to syllable weight (every syllable is open, §4; vowel quantity is positional — penult lengthening, coalescence, elision — and the single quantity-only pair Watkins reports, nidá·dza 'I came and am now here' / nidá:dza 'I came, but did not remain', is an aspect distinction that 'may, of course, be employed with any verb', §3b, so there is no lexical length contrast to condition stress); the stress is decidedly strong only where the penult also carries the high tone, so stress and pitch-accent fuse there. Separately, the penult vowel is lengthened when the word stands alone or is the last word of a sound group (§3b).
4462.srule: Not mentioned in Watkins 1937 (§5 'Pitch-accent and Stress', pp. 16-17, read in full with §3b p. 10, §4 p. 15 and §33 p. 86): Watkins describes one weak penultimate stress per word, strong only when fused with high tone on the penult, and writes stress only in ideophones; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

4463.dq: All word-level pitch processes in Nyang’i can be accounted for with reference to two tone levels: high and low.
4463.prule: No stress rule. Beer 2017 (pp. 40-42) describes Nyang'i word prosody as lexically specified but non-contrastive pitch, handled with tone formalisms: the pitch features of a root are not predictable from segmental or prosodic context or from position in the word, are consistent across utterances, and are never the sole means of contrast; duration and amplitude do not track pitch, so 'the prosodic system is not more meaningfully described as a stress system than as a tone system'. Surface tones H, L, F (F only in a closed final syllable), two underlying tones; 'High tone and low tone may occur at any position in a word'.

'Is Nyang’i, then, a tone language? 4465.heavy: Heavy = the 'major foot': CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr or CVrCrV (Vr, Cr = reduced vowel/consonant; a reduced segment 'receives less stress, is of shorter duration and is less clearly articulated', fn. 2). The unit is the foot, not the syllable: major feet are historically two CV syllables fused by reduction (kɔ+lɔ > kɔli) and are longer than one minor foot but shorter than two. Light = the CV minor foot. In syllable terms this approximates CVV (long vowel/diphthong) plus CVC-like fused disyllables (the reduced vowel of CVCrVr may go unarticulated, [kɔlʲ˺]); no existing value fits exactly, hence 'onset-or-other'.

4465.prule: Word prominence ('stress', non-contrastive, cued by duration and articulation) goes to the word's major foot, i.e. the heavy foot of shape CVV, CVʔV, CVCrVr or CVrCrV (e.g. /kabiɛlɛ/ 'finger' = minor ka + major biɛ + minor lɛ, stress on biɛ; /kɔli/ 'hand' one CVCrVr major foot); light CV minor feet are unstressed and 'usually' the single major foot carries the greatest stress; most words have exactly one major foot; in words composed solely of minor feet the primary stress falls on the initial foot (/pe/, /tɔgɔ/, /cogolo/).

4466.heavy: 'I define a syllable as strong if it either consist of more than two morae, or is the initial syllable of a word. Weak syllables, by contrast, are in non-initial position, and consist of at most two morae.' (p. 99; fn. 21: C(C), V and vowel length each weigh 0.5, summed and rounded to the nearest integer, halves up). By the letter of fn. 21 a closed short-vowel syllable is 2 morae, i.e. not 'more than two'; in the examples the effective contrast is nonetheless CV (weak) vs closed or long-vowelled syllables (CVC, CVCC, CVV: 'heavier', 'strong'), which take the non-initial stresses and, in the exceptional words, attract stress away from a light initial syllable. Weight conditions only the non-initial stresses and the exceptions, never the regular initial stress.
4466.prule: Regular pattern: the first syllable of every phonological word is stressed, regardless of syllable count, of whether the word begins with a vowel or a consonant, and of the weight of the initial syllable (the initial syllable counts as 'strong' by definition). Stress is non-contrastive and delimitative. Degrees of stress cannot be distinguished in the data, so all stressed syllables are marked alike; the initial stress is the invariant, quantity-insensitive component.
4466.srule: Further stresses (the source cannot distinguish degrees; all stresses are marked alike) fall on odd-numbered syllables counted from the initial: a non-final odd syllable (3rd, 5th) is stressed, a word-final odd syllable only if strong (more than two morae: closed or long-vowelled), so 'ba.ba.rli but 'ka.rriny.'kam, 'ku.rru.'lu.kun, 'wi.da.'ma.nga.'ran; in four-syllable roots a strong final may be stressed instead of a weak third ('ka.ja.na.'ngurr). Verb forms show a preference for the same stressed-unstressed alternation.
4466.quote: As in most Australian languages, stress is not phonemic in Nyulnyul: it does not serve a contrastive function, and no words are distinguished by different loci of stress. tn.quote: Le nzakara est un parler à tons. La différence de hauteur de réalisation de sons est pertinente; elle sert ordinairement à distinguer un mot d'un autre, d'où sa valeur sémantique: pi (bière) / pí (se coucher): bas / haut. Il faut noter que les tons nzakara présentent trois registres: bas, moyen et haut; donc trois tons ponctuels ou simples et deux tons modulés: un montant et un descendant qui sont pertinents. ... l'élément supra-segmentaire est le tonème: les tons ponctuels (bas, moyen et haut) et les tons modulés (montant et descendant).
tn.translation: Nzakara is a tone language. The difference in pitch at which sounds are realised is distinctive; it ordinarily serves to distinguish one word from another, hence its semantic value: pi (beer) / pí (lie down): low / high. Note that Nzakara tones show three registers: low, mid and high; thus three level or simple tones and two contour tones: a rising and a falling one, which are distinctive. ... the suprasegmental element is the toneme: the level tones (low, mid and high) and the contour tones (rising and falling).
tn.cite: Ebanda wa Kalema (1990). Esquisse phonologique du nzakara, un parler oubanguien. Annales Aequatoria 11: 189-201.
tn.locator: p. 198, sec. B 'Phonèmes supra-segmentaires'; last sentence from the Conclusion, p. 199
tn.note: Five tonemes: low, mid, high, rising (low-high), falling (high-low), with word examples; low left unmarked. Nothing on TBU, downstep or stress; p. 193: each vowel of an i+V sequence keeps its tone.

4468.tone: Welman p. 74: 'tone, or the pitch of the voice, is used to distinguish differences of meaning'; three provisional tones (normal, higher than normal, lower than normal), the last two marked by acute and grave accents; 'the relation of the tones to vowel-length and stress, cannot as yet be given'; the page closes by announcing a list of 'words in Nzima of the same form, but with different meanings, indicated by tone'. Welman p. 20 (D. Special Signs): 'A line over a vowel indicates that it is much prolonged'; 'The sign ' over a vowel means that the voice is raised to a higher tone than normal (see Chapter VI.—Tones).'; 'The sign ` over a vowel means that the voice is dropped to a lower tone than normal.' Welman pp. 107-108: the 1sg future negative differs from the positive 'by the pitch of the voice only, the negative being on a high tone'; a conjunctive form is 'Same form as Positive, distinction by tone'. Modern sources held (Nyame 2025 GJL 14(1); Nyame 2026 SKASE JTL 23(1); Amoh et al. 2023; Nyame & Ebule 2022) mark high and low tone on every Nzema example and never mention stress or accent (a full-text search of all 11 held: the only stress/accent hits about Nzema are the Welman p. 74 lines; the other hits are ordinary-English 'stress' or a generic Casali 1996 remark). No source states a stress or accent placement rule.

4469.heavy: Hunfalvy p. 50: 'hosszúság' (length), hedged: 'Úgy látszik, ezekben a' hosszúság kívánja meg a' hangsúlyt (mi ellenközik a' finn-ugor nyelv-jellemmel), vagy tévesztette az orosz írót. Ezt azért is gyanítani lehet, mert a' psa képző, melly eredetileg psaj, tehát hosszú, a' fosztó la előtt hangsúlyos' — the a of the stressed non-initial syllable in paltap, veśkat, horam, horaz, pazan, ńoga, jastandta, langamïmot and the suffix -psa (< psaj) draws the stress; no length marks are printed, stressed vowels are set in bold; vowel vs syllable length is not distinguished by Hunfalvy, but the psaj argument is about a vowel lengthened by a lost j. Nikolaeva 1995:32 (carried via Kashkin 2020:35): the second syllable is stressed when its vowel is long and wide (low) and the first syllable's vowel is short or long and narrow (high). Nikolaeva 1999 (carried via Normanskaja 2014:283): a syllable is heavy if it contains a long vowel, light if a short one. Honti 1984, pan-Khanty (carried via Normanskaja 2014): full vowel in the second syllable against a reduced one in the first, or a lower vowel in the second than in the first.
4469.dflt: first syllable (Hunfalvy's main rule; Nikolaeva 1999 via Normanskaja 2014: on the first light syllable when the word has no heavy one)
4469.prule: Main rule (Hunfalvy's 'fő szabály', stated twice, pp. 49-50): primary stress on the first syllable of the word regardless of its length. Deviations: words in final -a (jena, aga, hoźa, kinźa, pada, seda 'stb.'), imperatives (mana), and a set of nouns/participles (paltap, veśkat, horam, horaz, pazan, ńoga 'stb.', kept under suffixation: paltapla, veskatla, horazing, horazet) plus jastandta, langamïmot carry the stress on a later syllable; Hunfalvy explains these, with hedges, by length ('Úgy látszik, ezekben a' hosszúság kívánja meg a' hangsúlyt... vagy tévesztette az orosz írót') and generalises the explanation through the suffix -psa < psaj, 'tehát hosszú', which is stressed before privative -la (evilïpsala) where imila, mortotla, hurila are not. The modern Obdorsk description, reachable only second-hand: Nikolaeva 1995:32 (quoted verbatim in Kashkin 2020:35): stress mostly on the first syllable, but on the second when V1 is short or long-narrow (high) and V2 is long-wide (low); Nikolaeva 1999 as paraphrased by Normanskaja 2014:283: stress on the leftmost heavy (long-vowel) syllable, otherwise on the first (light) syllable.
4469.srule: Not mentioned in Hunfalvy 1875, 24. § 'Hangsúly', pp. 49-50 (the primary source). vnotes: Source ambiguous: On the catalog's closed list the article supports 'phrasal' (the only stress it describes is phrase stress: 'One phrase stress is assigned to each stress group in a given utterance', p. 5, landing syllable chosen by phonological / morphosyntactic / semantic-pragmatic hierarchies, p. 9, never by position in the word) and would also admit 'tonal' (three lexical tonemes high / low / extra high, p. 3-4, and no word-level stress-placement rule anywhere; the only 'syllable (word) stress' mention, p. 4, is about English via Lehiste). …
4470.dq: Phrase stress is realized over stress groups, which are usually smaller than pause groups (although the two may coincide over one single phrase). One phrase stress is assigned to each stress group in a given utterance.
4470.dloc: p. 5 (section 1 'Phrase stress in Obolo'); page = scan page + 2.
4470.prule: Phrase-level stress only. One phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group (a verb phrase with its subject, objects and modifiers; each serial verb and each indirect object a separate group; a place/time/manner complement; a detached or coordinated noun phrase), cued by extra-high F0, high amplitude and extra length (stressed vowels 215-245 ms vs 118-181 ms unstressed, table p. 5). Which syllable of the group carries it is not fixed by position in the word: it gravitates to underlyingly non-low syllables and group boundaries (phonological), to extra-high-toned verbal prefixes, the first morpheme of a place/time/manner complement, extra-high verb roots and prominent subject NPs (morphosyntactic), and follows verb focus (semantic-pragmatic); certain extra-high grammatical morphemes (negative ka, future ma/mo/me, 3sg completive i, question words, interjections, imperatives) are automatically stressed. No word-level stress position is stated anywhere.
4470.srule: Not mentioned in Faraclas 1984 (JWAL 14(1): 3-17, whole article read): stress is phrasal only, one phrase stress per syntactically defined stress group; no word-level primary or secondary stress is described (p. 11 says only that pitch may be raised on syllables adjacent to the phrase-stressed syllable and that the stress sometimes spreads evenly over two or three syllables).
4470.quote: In Obolo, each syllable of a noun is assigned one tone lexically, while each verb stem is assigned a single tone (high or low) which is distributed suprasegmentally over however many syllables it may contain. The systems of lexical tone and downdrift, however, coexist and interact with other suprasegmental systems, including a system of phrasal stress. [p. 4] ... In Obolo, the speech chain divides itself into several units of varying length which correspond to the different units to which suprasegmental features are assigned. Intonation patterns are realized over pause groups, which are usual…
4470.loc: pp. 4-5 (section 1 'Phrase stress in Obolo') and p. 9; further pp. 10-13 (automatically stressed morphemes, stress spreading, suspension of non-initial phrase stress, lexical extra high). Scan has; page = scan page + 2.
4470.idn: Source data are from the Western dialects of Obolo: Faraclas 1984 fn. 1 (p. 16) says much of the material is included in his 'A Phonology of the Western Dialects of Obolo' (forthcoming), and his 1982 JWAL 12(2) article is likewise on 'the Western dialects of Obolo'. The article treats Obolo…
4470.exq_: No word-level rule, so no word-level exceptions. Modifications of the phrase-stress rule the source itself states (p. 11): 'In some cases, the stress seems to distribute itself evenly over two or even three syllables.' and 'Under information-question, imperative, negative, exclamatory, hypothetical…
4470.tone: Obolo has three tonemes (high, low, extra high; earlier analyses had five, p. 3). Nouns: one lexical tone per syllable; verb stems: a single H or L distributed over the stem (p. 4). Extra high is both a lexical toneme and the main cue of phrase stress (p. 4); under phrase stress level tones become glides (extra high > fall to high, high > fall to low, low > rise to high). Extra high never occurs on verb stems (p. 13) and occurs on noun stems 'in cases where there is no apparent reason to postulate accent or stress at any level' (p. 13, scan with edge-clipped letters). The article never speaks of word stress or word accent; stress is treated as phrasal throughout, interacting with lexical tone and downdrift.

4471.tone: Agnew & Pike 1957 describe contrastive pitch with two tone levels (high/low) on each vowel, low much more frequent, optional downdrift of low tone through the utterance, HL/LH glides on long vocoids (p. 27), and tone alternations marking mode, tense, person and stem morphophonemics; they never use the word 'stress', and 'accent' only as the name of the diacritic ('the acute accent over a vowel indicates high tone'). Leach 1969/2008 (Vocabulario ocaina, 'Aclaraciones acerca del alfabeto ocaina (dialecto uvohsa)', p. 163, read in the archive.org scan of the 2008 ed.) treats the same acute as an orthographic 'acento' like Spanish, 'indicando la sílaba o sílabas que llevan la mayor fuerza de voz', read 'en tono relativamente elevado a las sílabas no acentuadas'; unaccented words are read 'con tono de voz relativamente bajo y con acento menguante en la primera sílaba: foojo la casa, fóójo tu casa'. On either account the prominence is lexically placed and realized as high pitch, so the record is tonal/pitch-accent with no positional stress rule.

4472.prule: Stress (the 'acento': greater intensity plus vowel length on the stressed vowel) is placed 'by the same rules as in Spanish', i.e. it is lexically specified and written only where it departs from the Spanish default: unmarked vowel-final disyllables are stressed on the first (penultimate) vowel (lari 'clothes', begu 'comb'), words with a written accent on the final vowel (dumí 'money', laní 'fiesta'). No phonological predictor is given (lari vs laní have the same CVCV shape), so stress is lexical with a penultimate default for vowel-final words. Separately, the language has three lexical tones (low, high, rising), unwritten.

4474.prule: No word-stress rule. All Lower Cross languages (Okobo is one of the 19 in Connell's sample, with first-hand 1988 field data) have two lexical tones, H and L, plus phonologically significant downstep, i.e. a two-tone terraced-level tone system; Connell finds no true evidence for word (verb-root) stress, rejecting Ward's 1933 Efik analysis, and calls LC 'a non-stress language', while conceding likely phrasal stress and stress at compound-word junctures (investigated only for Obolo by Faraclas 1984b). No syllable position is ever named as stressed.

In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. tn.quote: The system that exists throughout LC is one of two basic tones, High (H = ') and Low (L = v), which may combine on a given syllable (with restricted and varying distribution) to give Falling (H+L = "), and less frequently, Rising (L+H = ") tones. ... In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep (Ds = !); i.e., the non-predictable lowering of H following another H, which has the effect of lowering the 'ceiling' for subsequent H tone realization. Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages.
